lessons.title: Lesson 1: Where AI shows up in games, and how it can coach you
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Name ways AI is used in games and ways an AI assistant can help you practice.
This lesson builds toward: Thinking about a game you play, you will identify ways AI is used inside games and what an AI assistant can and cannot do to help you practice, getting at least 3 of 4 right.
Games have used AI for a long time. The computer-controlled characters you play against, the system that matches you with players near your skill, and tools that catch cheaters can all use AI.
An AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini is different. It cannot see your screen or play for you, but it can help you think: set goals, plan practice, explain strategy ideas and find patterns in notes you give it.
It does not know every game patch or update, and it can be wrong. Check strategy tips against the game's official notes, your team captain or coach, and your own results.
Words to know:
- AI: artificial intelligence: computer programs that do tasks that usually need a person.
- Matchmaking: the system that picks who you play with or against.
- Patch: an update that changes a game.
Try it now: Write down the game you play most and three things in it you would like to get better at. Circle the one that matters most to you right now.
You can now name ways AI is used in games and explain what an AI assistant can and cannot do as a practice coach.

check.q: Which of these can use AI inside a game?
check.why: Computer players, matchmaking and anti-cheat tools can all use AI.

check.q: AI tells you a strategy that seems off after a new update. What do you do?
options: Use it in your next ranked match without checking
Check it against the official game notes or your coach
Ask a stranger for your login
check.why: AI may not know the latest patch, so check its tips against official notes and your results.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Setting a goal and building a practice plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to turn one goal into a weekly practice plan that fits your life.
This lesson builds toward: Given one skill to improve and your real schedule, you will build a one-week practice plan with AI using a small, measurable goal and short drills, fitting around school, homework and sleep.
Getting better comes from practicing one thing on purpose, not just playing more. A good goal is small and measurable: "Land more of my shots in practice mode" or "Call out enemy positions every round", not "get good".
Give the AI your game, your goal, your current level and your real schedule. For example: "I play Rocket League. I want better aerial hits. I can practice 30 minutes on 4 school nights after homework. Make a simple one-week plan with short drills and a way to track progress."
Put school, homework, sleep and family time in first. Esports players at every level take breaks, stretch and rest their eyes. A plan you can actually keep beats a huge plan you quit.
Step by step:
- Choose one small, measurable goal.
- Tell the AI your game, goal, level and real free time.
- Ask for a one-week plan with short drills and a way to track progress.
- Check it leaves time for school, homework and sleep.
- Ask for one change if it is too much.
Words to know:
- Measurable goal: a goal you can check with a number or a yes or no.
- Drill: a short exercise that practices one skill.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for a one-week practice plan for the skill you circled in Lesson 1, using your real schedule. Ask it to make the plan shorter if it takes more than 30 to 45 minutes a day.
You can now turn one gaming goal into a realistic weekly practice plan with an AI assistant.

options: Playing more hours without a goal
check.why: Getting better comes from practicing one thing on purpose.

check.q: You want to "get good." How do you turn that into a better goal?
options: Make it small and measurable, like landing more shots in practice mode
check.why: A small, measurable goal lets you see real progress.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reviewing a match with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write notes from a match and use AI to find a pattern and suggest a drill.
This lesson builds toward: After playing or watching a match, you will write three match notes and ask AI to find a pattern and suggest one drill, with no other players' usernames or private messages.
Top players review their matches. After a match, or while watching a replay if your game has one, write three short notes: one thing that went well, one mistake, and when it happened.
Paste the notes into an AI assistant and ask: "Here are my notes from three matches. What patterns do you see, and what is one drill that would help?" The AI is good at spotting repeats you might miss.
Keep notes about the game, not about other people. Do not paste other players' usernames, private messages or anything personal. And be kind to yourself: the goal is to learn, not to feel bad.
Step by step:
- Play or watch a replay of one match.
- Write three notes: something good, a mistake, and when it happened.
- Collect notes from two or three matches.
- Ask the AI for patterns and one drill.
- Add the drill to your practice plan.
Words to know:
- Replay: a recording of a match you can watch again.
- Pattern: something that happens again and again.
Try it now: Play one match, write three notes, and ask an AI assistant what it notices and what one drill it suggests. Add that drill to your plan.
You can now review a match with notes and use AI to find a pattern and choose a drill.

check.q: What is the purpose of reviewing a match?
options: To learn from what went well and what went wrong
check.why: Reviewing helps you learn; the goal is not to feel bad.

check.q: Your notes include a teammate's username and chat. What do you do before pasting them into AI?
options: Remove the username and chat and keep notes about the game
check.why: Keep notes about the game, not about other people.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Teams, safety and esports futures

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Talking well with your team
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to help write short team callouts and a clear club or team message.
This lesson builds toward: For your team or club, you will create a list of short callouts and a friendly team message in your own voice, keeping callouts short and calm and the message under 80 words.
Good teams talk clearly and kindly. Callouts are short words the team agrees on, like "two left" or "rotating mid". Short, calm callouts beat long or angry ones.
An AI assistant can help you make a callout list for your game, or write a message for your school club: practice times, what you will work on, and a reminder to be respectful. Ask: "Write a short, friendly message to my school esports club about Thursday practice. Keep it under 80 words."
If a teammate makes a mistake, focus on the next play, not blame. Teams that stay positive play better and have more fun.
Step by step:
- List the most common moments in your game that need a callout.
- Ask the AI for short, clear callout words for each.
- Agree on the list with your team.
- Use AI to draft a short, friendly team or club message.
- Read it, change it to sound like you, then share it.
Words to know:
- Callout: a short word or phrase that tells teammates what is happening.
- Esports: organized, competitive video gaming, often with teams and leagues.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to help you make a list of five callouts for your game. Then have it draft a short message to your team or club about your next practice, and rewrite it in your own voice.
You can now create clear team callouts and a friendly team message with AI's help.

options: A long speech after the match
A short phrase that tells teammates what is happening
check.why: Callouts are short words the team agrees on, like "two left".

check.q: AI drafted your club message, but it sounds stiff. What do you do?
options: Rewrite it so it sounds like you before sharing
check.why: Read and change AI drafts so they sound like you.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Gaming safely and fairly
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot cheats, scams and unsafe chats, and know what to do.
This lesson builds toward: When you meet cheats, scams or unsafe chats, you will refuse cheats and scams, keep private details out of chats, and block, report and tell a trusted adult, sharing no login, code or personal details.
Cheats such as aimbots or hacked files break a game's rules and can get your account banned. Sites that promise free game currency, skins or "AI cheats" often steal accounts or install harmful software. Never download them or give your login to anyone.
Be careful in chats. Do not share your real name, school, address, phone number or photos with people you only know online. If someone pressures you, asks for secrets, or makes you uncomfortable, block them, report them in the game, and tell a parent, guardian or trusted adult.
Games carry age ratings. In the United States the ESRB rates games, for example T (Teen) for about 13 and up and M (Mature) for 17 and up. Talk with your family about which games and how much screen time are right for you.
Step by step:
- Never use cheats or download "free currency" tools.
- Never give your login or the code sent to your phone to anyone.
- Keep your real name, school and address out of chats.
- Block, report and tell a trusted adult when something feels wrong.
- Check a game's age rating with your family.
Words to know:
- Aimbot: a cheat that aims for you; it breaks game rules.
- Ban: when a game blocks your account for breaking rules.
- Age rating: a label that says which ages a game is meant for.
Official sources:
- ESRB: Ratings guide
Try it now: Open the settings of a game or platform you use and find where to block and report a player. Then look up the age rating of your favorite game on the ESRB website.
You can now spot cheats, account scams and unsafe chats, and know how to block, report and get help.

check.q: What usually happens on sites that promise free game currency or skins?
options: They often steal accounts or install harmful software
check.why: Free-currency and cheat sites often steal accounts or install harmful software.

check.q: An online player keeps asking for your photo and says to keep it secret. What do you do?
options: Block, report and tell a parent, guardian or trusted adult
check.why: Pressure and secrets are warning signs; block, report and tell a trusted adult.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Esports careers and putting it all together
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explore jobs around esports and complete your practice plan and match review.
This lesson builds toward: Using AI and a trusted source, you will list jobs in esports besides pro player and check one with a counselor or a real job listing, naming the skills the job needs.
Only a few people become professional players, but esports needs many other people: coaches, team managers, shoutcasters who commentate matches, video editors, graphic designers, event organizers, and the people who design and test games.
Ask an AI assistant: "What jobs exist in esports besides being a pro player? What school subjects and clubs help with each?" Then check the answers with a school counselor or a real job listing, because AI can be out of date.
Many schools have esports clubs or teams. If yours does not, a club advisor or teacher may help you start one. Now put it all together: goal, plan, match review and a team message.
Step by step:
- Ask AI to list esports jobs and the skills each needs.
- Pick one job that interests you.
- Check it with a counselor or a real job listing.
- Complete your goal, plan, match review and team message.
Words to know:
- Shoutcaster: a person who commentates esports matches live.
- Event organizer: a person who plans and runs tournaments.
Try it now: Final task: build a one-week practice plan with AI that fits around school and sleep, review one match with three notes, ask the AI for a pattern and one drill, and write a short team or club message about what you will work on next.
You can now use AI as a practice coach, game safely and fairly, and name esports jobs beyond being a pro player.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Goal and plan The goal is vague, like "get good", or there is no plan. One small, measurable goal and a one-week plan with short drills. The plan includes a way to track progress each day. Balanced with life The plan cuts into school, homework or sleep. School, homework and sleep come first, and practice fits around them. Also includes breaks, stretching or eye rest. Match review Fewer than three notes, or notes about other people. Three notes (good, mistake, when) and one AI-suggested drill added to the plan. Notes from two or more matches, with the pattern the AI found explained in the learner's words. Team message The message is missing, long or unkind. A short, friendly message about what the team will work on, in the learner's own voice. Also includes an agreed callout list. Safe and fair The plan or notes include private details, or mention cheats. No private details anywhere, and no cheats or unsafe tools. The learner can show where to block and report in their game. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which of these is an esports job besides pro player?
check.why: Esports needs coaches, managers, shoutcasters, editors, designers and event organizers.

check.q: AI lists esports jobs and the skills they need. What do you do next?
options: Check one job with a school counselor or a real job listing
check.why: AI can be out of date, so check with a counselor or a real listing.
